---
title: Recipes
---

Short, copy-ready versions of the jobs most apps need. Each assumes [`set_url_base()`](../reference/set_url_base.qmd) and [`login()`](../reference/login.qmd) already ran at startup, and each links to the guide page that explains the pieces.

## Handle a signup form

Someone ticks "send me the newsletter" on your signup form. They might already be a subscriber (they bought something last year), might be blocklisted (they unsubscribed and came back), or might be new. One function covers all three.

```python
import listmonk
from listmonk.models import SubscriberStatuses

NEWSLETTER = 7


def subscribe_to_newsletter(email: str, name: str, source: str) -> None:
    sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email(email)

    if sub is None:
        listmonk.create_subscriber(email, name, list_ids={NEWSLETTER}, pre_confirm=True,
                                   attribs={'signup_source': source})
        return

    sub.attribs['signup_source'] = source
    # They asked again, so re-enable them even if they had unsubscribed before.
    listmonk.update_subscriber(sub, add_to_lists={NEWSLETTER}, status=SubscriberStatuses.enabled)
```

`pre_confirm=True` because your form collected consent; drop it to let Listmonk run double opt-in instead. The explicit `status=` matters: without it `update_subscriber()` keeps whatever status the person has, which is the right default everywhere except here. See [Subscribers](subscribers.qmd) and [Lists and segmentation](lists.qmd#single-and-double-opt-in).

## Handle an unsubscribe link

Your app has its own unsubscribe page. Decide whether the click means "take me off this one list" or "never email me again"; they are different calls.

```python
def unsubscribe(email: str, list_id: int | None = None) -> bool:
    sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email(email)
    if sub is None:
        return False

    if list_id is not None:
        listmonk.update_subscriber(sub, remove_from_lists={list_id})   # just this list
    else:
        listmonk.block_subscriber(sub)                                  # everything, for good
    return True
```

`block_subscriber()` keeps the record with a `blocklisted` status, so a later import or sync cannot accidentally resurrect them. Use `delete_subscriber()` only for a genuine "forget me" request. See [Pausing, unsubscribing, and deleting](subscribers.qmd#pausing-unsubscribing-and-deleting).

## Send a receipt with a PDF

Receipts go to whoever paid, subscriber or not, so use external mode and carry everything the template needs in `template_data`.

```python
from pathlib import Path

RECEIPT_TEMPLATE = 4  # a 'tx' template


def send_receipt(email: str, order_id: int, total: str, pdf_path: Path) -> bool:
    return listmonk.send_transactional_email(
        email,
        RECEIPT_TEMPLATE,
        subscriber_mode='external',
        template_data={'order_id': order_id, 'total': total},
        attachments=[pdf_path],
        content_type='html',
        altbody=f'Thanks for order {order_id}. Your receipt is attached.',
    )
```

In external mode only `{{ .Subscriber.Email }}` is available, so the template reads the order number as `{{ .Tx.Data.order_id }}`. See [Transactional email](transactional-email.qmd#people-who-are-not-subscribers).

## Send a password reset

Same idea, minus the attachment. Use `fallback` if most of your users are subscribers and you still want their name available when they are:

```python
RESET_TEMPLATE = 3


def send_password_reset(email: str, reset_url: str) -> bool:
    return listmonk.send_transactional_email(
        email,
        RESET_TEMPLATE,
        subscriber_mode='fallback',
        template_data={'reset_url': reset_url},
        content_type='html',
    )
```

Remember that in `fallback` mode the subscriber fields other than the email are empty when the lookup fails, so write the template to work with `{{ .Tx.Data.reset_url }}` and a generic greeting.

## Sync your user table into a list

A nightly job that makes sure every active customer is on the "customers" list, creating anyone Listmonk has not seen yet.

```python
CUSTOMERS = 9


def sync_customers(users: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> None:
    """users is a list of (email, name) pairs from your own database."""
    ids: list[int] = []
    for email, name in users:
        sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email(email)
        if sub is None:
            sub = listmonk.create_subscriber(email, name, pre_confirm=True)
        ids.append(sub.id)

    for start in range(0, len(ids), 500):
        listmonk.add_subscribers_to_lists(ids[start:start + 500], [CUSTOMERS])
```

`add_subscribers_to_lists()` takes IDs, de-duplicates them, and returns `False` rather than raising on an error, so check it if you need to. People already on the list are simply left there. This loop makes one lookup per user; for a very large table, pull everyone with `subscribers()` once and build a dict by email instead. See [Lists and segmentation](lists.qmd#membership).

## Send a newsletter from code

Create, attach, test, then start. Keep yourself on a private staff list so the test send always has a known subscriber to go to.

```python
from pathlib import Path

NEWSLETTER = 7
STAFF = ['you@example.com']


def send_newsletter(subject: str, markdown_body: str, chart: Path) -> int:
    media = listmonk.upload_media(chart)
    campaign = listmonk.create_campaign(
        name=subject, subject=subject, list_ids={NEWSLETTER},
        content_type='markdown', body=markdown_body, media_ids=[media.id],
    )
    listmonk.test_campaign(campaign.id, STAFF)
    input(f'Test sent to {STAFF}. Press Enter to send campaign {campaign.id} to the list...')
    listmonk.start_campaign(campaign.id)
    return campaign.id
```

Swap the `input()` for whatever approval step fits your workflow. To schedule instead of sending now, pass `send_at=` to `create_campaign()` and move the campaign to `CampaignStatuses.scheduled` with `set_campaign_status()`. See [Campaigns](campaigns.qmd).

## Add a health check to your app

```python
import httpx2


def listmonk_ok() -> bool:
    return listmonk.is_healthy(timeout_config=httpx2.Timeout(timeout=3))
```

`is_healthy()` never raises; it returns `False` for an unreachable server, a rejected credential, or a client that was never configured, so it is safe to call from a readiness probe. The short timeout keeps the probe fast when the mail server is down. See [Errors and troubleshooting](error-handling.qmd#timeouts).
